transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Lately I just feel like the future doesn’t hold much for me and that the meaningful part of my life is already over. My primary care doctor noticed this shift in my outlook during my annual wellness visit and suggested I come speak with you.
How long have you been feeling this way, and was there a specific event or change in your life that seemed to trigger these feelings?

This low, hopeless feeling has been hanging around pretty steadily for a little over three years now. It really started after the initial excitement of my retirement from biomedical engineering wore off, and I began to feel like my current activities don't really matter compared to what I achieved during my career.
Before these past three years, have you ever had other periods in your life where you felt deeply depressed or down for weeks or months at a time?

No, I haven't really experienced periods of feeling deeply depressed or down like this prior to my retirement. This low feeling is a completely new experience for me that only began a few years ago after I left my career. Before that, I was always very engaged and motivated.
During these past three years of feeling low, have you also noticed other changes like trouble sleeping, low energy, changes in your appetite, or difficulty concentrating?

I’ve definitely noticed that my energy is quite low, and even a morning of light errands or a couple of hours in my studio leaves me feeling like I've hit a wall and need to sit in my chair for the afternoon. As for my sleep, appetite, or concentration, I haven't really noticed any significant changes in those areas. It's mostly just this persistent fatigue that sets in very easily.
During these past three years, have there been any periods lasting two months or more where you felt completely back to your normal self and free of these feelings?

No, I haven't had any periods like that where I felt back to my normal self. This low, gray, and hopeless feeling has been a steady, constant presence over the last three years without any real break.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in almost all of your usual activities, like your studio work, or do you still find some enjoyment in them when you have the energy?

Yes, I've largely lost that sense of interest and pleasure. It feels like the volume on everything enjoyable has been turned way down. Even when I am painting in my studio or attending the chess club, I feel like I'm just going through the motions without really feeling much of anything.
During this difficult time, have you had any thoughts of death, or felt that you would be better off dead?
No, I haven't had any thoughts of death or wanting to hurt myself. Even though I feel like I'm just marking time, I've never wished I were dead or felt that way.
During these past three years, have you struggled with feelings of worthlessness, or have you found yourself feeling excessively guilty or blaming yourself for things?

I haven't really felt excessive guilt or blamed myself for anything. It's not so much a feeling of worthlessness, but rather that my current daily activities just lack the sense of purpose and importance that my career used to have.

During these past three years, was there ever a period of a few weeks where your symptoms became significantly more intense, perhaps making it hard to take care of yourself or perform basic daily tasks?

No, I haven't had any intense spikes where I couldn't take care of myself or handle daily tasks. It has just been a very steady, continuous, low-grade gray feeling where I keep going through the motions. I still manage to get things done, it's just that the feeling itself never really changes.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent, continuous low-grade depressed mood ('low, gray, and hopeless feeling') lasting for over three years since his retirement. He reports associated low energy/fatigue and a marked loss of interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia). He has not had any symptom-free periods lasting longer than two months, and he denies any history of severe major depressive episodes, mania, or hypomania. This clinical presentation perfectly aligns with the diagnostic criteria for Dysthymia (F34.1).
